sections.h2: What kind of city is Bridgeport, Connecticut?
sections.html:
Bridgeport is a Fairfield County city and port at the mouth of the Pequonnock River on Long Island Sound. It covers 19.4 square miles, of which 16.0 are land, and sits at an elevation of only about 3.3 feet, with about 9,290 people per square mile.

The Census Bureau counted 148,654 residents in 2020. The city became a town in 1821 and a city in 1836, and it operates under a mayor and city council. Its name comes from the drawbridge over the Pequonnock, and its motto, Industria Crescimus, means "by industry we thrive."

Because the city is low, dense and on the water, a Bridgeport sale often turns on details that a hill-town sale never raises, such as basements, drainage and insurance.

Bridgeport is usually described in five areas: Downtown, the East Side, the North End, the South End and the West Side. Each has several named neighborhoods, and buyers think in those names.

  • Downtown: the Hollow, McLevy Green and the downtown north and south districts.
  • East Side: Steel Point, the East End, Newfield, Mill Hill and Pleasure Beach.
  • North End: Lake Forest, Lake Success, Brooklawn, St. Vincent, Old Town Road and the Reservoir area.
  • South End: Seaside Park and Soundgate.
  • West Side: Black Rock, the West End and St. Mary's by the Sea.

Use the neighborhood name when you describe your house to anyone. A Black Rock address and a Lower East Side address are different places, and a direct buyer will price each one on its own terms.

sections.h2: How did Bridgeport's history shape its housing?
sections.html:
Bridgeport's first documented European settlement dates to 1644 at Black Rock Harbor, and the city grew through shipbuilding, rail and heavy manufacturing. Manufacturing stayed the mainstay of the local economy until the 1970s.

In 1852, P. T. Barnum and William Noble began developing East Bridgeport across the river, with homes, shops and factories around East Main Street. Harvey Hubbell founded Hubbell Incorporated in the city in 1888. In 1864 Barnum, Noble and Nathaniel Wheeler donated the shoreline land that became Seaside Park, and both Seaside Park and Beardsley Park were designed by Frederick Law Olmsted. Together those parks gave Bridgeport the nickname the Park City, and today the city counts 35 public parks on about 1,300 acres.

Much of the city grew up around its factories and parks, with later redevelopment layered on top.

sections.h2: What is changing in Bridgeport's downtown and waterfront?
sections.html:
Redevelopment has been a long project in Bridgeport and it continues. The city approved a new master plan in 2009 and updated it in April 2019.

  • Artists' lofts opened in the former Read's Department Store on Broad Street in 2004.
  • The 117-unit Citytrust bank building on Main Street became rentals.
  • The condominium conversion at Bijou Square went ahead after the Great Recession paused two large mixed-use projects.
  • The Steel Point project on the lower East Side produced a big box retailer in 2013, with a marina and plans for apartments.

Projects like these can lift interest near downtown and the waterfront, while streets farther out may see little change. If your house is near a redevelopment area, mention it, because investors track those boundaries.

sections.h2: How does Bridgeport bill property tax?
sections.html:
The city says taxes are assessed as of October 1, levied the following July 1, and paid in two installments on July 1 and January 1. Liens are filed on the last day of the fiscal year, June 30.

For fiscal year 2026-2027, the Bridgeport mill rate is 27.95 mills on real estate and personal property and 31.75 mills on motor vehicles. One mill equals $1 of tax for each $1,000 of assessment. The city's example uses a 70 percent assessed value, so the bill is computed on the assessment rather than on the market price of the house.

When you sell, ask the Bridgeport tax collector for a payoff statement for your parcel. Unpaid installments and any lien must be settled from the proceeds, and a bill that was mailed to a previous owner or a mortgage company is still your obligation if it is unpaid.

sections.h2: What does the coast mean for a Bridgeport house?
sections.html:
Bridgeport has a mild coastal climate with about 44.9 inches of precipitation a year and around 29 inches of snow on average. Hurricanes are infrequent but real: landfalls on the Connecticut coast occurred in 1903, 1938, 1944, 1954, 1960, 1985 and, with Hurricane Sandy, 2012.

For sellers, that history means flood and wind questions come up in showings and inspections, especially for a city that sits only a few feet above sea level. Pull any insurance declarations, elevation certificates or storm repair records you have. A direct buyer will still look closely at the foundation and the mechanical systems, but a tidy paper trail shortens the conversation.

sections.h2: What taxes and exemptions apply at a Bridgeport closing?
sections.html:
A conveyance tax applies when the deed goes on the land records and the price reaches $2,000. The Department of Revenue Services expects the return, Form OP-236, to be filed and any tax paid when the deed is recorded, and the town code for Bridgeport is 015.

The statute sets the state rate at three-quarters of one percent for most homes, plus one-fourth of one percent to the municipality. A targeted investment community may add up to one-fourth of one percent more, so ask the Bridgeport Town Clerk which rate applies.

  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence is listed as an exempt conveyance.
  • So is the sale of a principal residence when the price cannot cover the mortgages and priority liens.
  • A property in a designated enterprise zone can claim a state exemption, but it is not exempt from the town portion.

Exemptions need the right code on the return, so check with the closing attorney before you rely on one.

sections.h2: Selling a Bridgeport house: list, sell yourself or take a cash offer
sections.html:
A listing can bring the highest price when the house is clean, updated and easy to show. It also brings commissions, prep work and a wait for a buyer's mortgage and appraisal.

A direct cash sale is faster and simpler for houses that need work, for owners who inherited a property, for landlords tired of a vacant or occupied unit and for families who must move soon. When a house needs updating, a cash buyer prices the repairs into the offer.

Whichever way you go, compare the net amount you would actually receive, not only the headline price. Commissions, repairs, carrying costs and weeks of mortgage and tax payments all reduce a listing's net.

faqs.q: What is the Bridgeport mill rate for real estate?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2026-2027 the city lists 27.95 mills on real estate and personal property, and 31.75 mills on motor vehicles. One mill equals $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessment.

faqs.q: When are Bridgeport property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due in two installments, July 1 and January 1. The city assesses as of October 1 and files liens on June 30, the last day of its fiscal year.

faqs.q: Do I have to fix my Bridgeport house before selling?
faqs.a: No. A direct buyer can purchase the house as it stands, and the offer reflects the condition. If you list instead, buyers and lenders may ask for repairs after the inspection.

faqs.q: Is a deed in lieu of foreclosure taxed in Bridgeport?
faqs.a: The state lists a deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence among exempt conveyances. Confirm how the exemption applies with the Bridgeport Town Clerk and your attorney before closing.

faqs.q: Which Bridgeport office handles property assessments?
faqs.a: The Bridgeport Tax Assessor sets assessed values, and the Tax Collector bills and collects payments. Contact both for a payoff figure and assessment details before you sell.
